_authoring_notes: Every question needs a matching entry in answer_key.json, keyed '<taskid>.<questionid>'.
kind: text | number | choice | ordering | command | written

context: follow-up | same-scenario | new-context. Shown above the question so a candidate knows whether it builds on the previous one. Omit for the first question in a task; others default to same-scenario.

meta.title: Sync - Junior IT Infrastructure Technician
meta.intro: This is a practical exercise. Each task shows you output from a system and asks you some questions about it. Some answers are a single value, some are a command you would run, and some are a few sentences in your own words. Nothing here needs knowledge of our specific tools - it is all readable from what is in front of you, plus general Linux and hardware sense.

tasks.title: Clearing a disk before it leaves the building
tasks.scenario:
A decommissioned disk has to be securely cleared before it leaves the facility. These five steps are in the wrong order.

  A. Run wipefs -a on the device to clear filesystem and partition-table signatures.
  B. Run sgdisk --zap-all on the device to destroy the GPT and MBR structures.
  C. Confirm the serial number matches the work order, and that nothing is mounted or in use on the device.
  D. Run kpartx -d to remove any device-mapper partition mappings for the device.
  E. Re-read the device and confirm it reports no signatures and no partitions.

questions.prompt: Put the five steps in the correct order, as letters separated by commas (for example B,A,E,C,D).
Why does the step you put first belong first? One or two sentences.

tasks.title: A filesystem that is full, but is not
tasks.scenario: An alert fires for a full filesystem on an application host. You log in and collect the following.

artifacts.label: on the host
artifacts.body:
$ df -h /var
Filesystem             Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/mapper/vg0-var     40G   40G     0 100% /var

$ du -sh /var
12G     /var

$ systemctl status rsyslog --no-pager | head -4
* rsyslog.service - System Logging Service
     Loaded: loaded (/usr/lib/systemd/system/rsyslog.service; enabled)
     Active: active (running) since Mon 2026-08-03 09:41:22 EDT; 7 weeks 2 days ago
   Main PID: 1184 (rsyslogd)

questions.prompt: df reports 40G used and du reports 12G. What is the most likely explanation? Answer with a single letter.
choices: A. du is only counting files owned by root
B. A running process is still holding a deleted file open
C. The filesystem is corrupt and needs to be checked
D. Reserved blocks account for the difference

questions.prompt: Write a command that would help you identify the file or process responsible.
How would you reclaim the space, and what would you check or who would you ask before doing it? Two or three sentences.

tasks.title: Capacity arithmetic
tasks.scenario:
Our Ceph pools use erasure coding. A pool is configured with k=8 data chunks and m=3 parity chunks, so usable capacity is:

  usable = raw * k / (k + m)

The pool sits on 14.0 PiB of raw disk. You do not need to know anything about Ceph to answer this - the formula is all you need.

questions.prompt: What is the usable capacity in PiB, to one decimal place?
The pool is currently 78% full. How many PiB of usable space remain? One decimal place.

tasks.title: Everyday Linux and networking
tasks.scenario: Four short questions. No system output for these - answer from what you know.

questions.prompt: A service called collector.service is misbehaving since the machine last booted. Write a single command that shows its log output for the current boot only.
Write a command that shows whether that service is currently running and when it last started.

A new host is configured with address 10.20.30.15, netmask 255.255.255.0, and default gateway 10.20.31.1. It can reach other hosts in its own rack but nothing outside it. What is wrong? Answer with a single letter.
choices: B. The gateway is outside the host's own subnet
C. The host address is a broadcast address
D. Nothing is wrong; the switch port must be down

questions.prompt: You have racked a new server and cabled it, but it does not appear on the network. Without touching any configuration yet, list the things you would check, roughly in the order you would check them.

tasks.title: Asking someone else to do the work
tasks.scenario: A disk has failed in a facility you cannot get to today. The colocation provider offers a remote hands service: their technician will go to the cage and do what you ask, but they have never seen our equipment, they will not log into anything, and every round of questions costs you an hour.

questions.prompt: Write the remote hands request. Assume the replacement disk is already on site. Include everything their technician needs to do the job correctly on the first attempt, and say what you want them to report back.

tasks.title: Handing it over
tasks.scenario: It is the end of your shift. The disk in task 1 has been replaced, but the multipath problem in task 2 is still unresolved and you are out of time. The technician taking over has not seen any of this.

questions.prompt: Write the handover note you would leave on the ticket: what you did, where things stand now, what is still outstanding, and what you would do next. Five to ten sentences.

tasks.title: Accounts and access
tasks.scenario: Three questions about how access is handled on Linux systems.

questions.prompt: On a standard Linux system, how are user passwords stored in /etc/shadow? Answer with a single letter.
choices: A. Encrypted with a system-wide key, so they can be decrypted when needed
B. Hashed with a per-user salt, so the original cannot be recovered
C. In plain text, protected only by the file permissions
D. Encrypted with each user's own password as the key

questions.prompt: Why is it done that way rather than the other way? Two or three sentences.
A server accepts SSH connections with a username and password. What, if anything, would you change to bring it in line with good practice, and why?

tasks.title: Monitoring and incidents
tasks.scenario: Two questions about alerting and what happens when things break.

questions.prompt: What separates a good monitor or alert from a bad one? Describe the qualities a good one has, and what makes a bad one worse than no alert at all.
During an outage, what do you think is the hardest part of handling it? And once service is restored, what still needs to happen?
